title: Fitting a wireless doorbell push and chime unit
subtitle: Fix a battery-powered wireless push button at the door and pair it with a plug-in or battery chime unit inside the house
excerpt: How to fit a wireless doorbell. Covers choosing a position for the push button, fixing it to the door frame or wall, pairing it with the chime receiver, and adjusting the volume and chime tone.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK consumer electronics installation guidance (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A doorbell system in which the push button contains a battery and a radio transmitter. Pressing the button sends a radio signal to a receiver (the chime unit) plugged into a mains socket inside the house. The chime unit requires no bell wire run from the door; the push button is entirely self-contained.

content.text: needs no bell wire run from the door to the chime; the push button runs on a battery and sends a radio signal. Fix the button, pair the units, and the doorbell works. The job takes about 15 minutes.

Fix the push button on the door frame at about 1350 mm from the ground, on the same side as the door latch (not the hinge side). This height suits most visitors and is accessible for wheelchair users. Fix to the door frame, not to the door itself: a button on the door swings away as the door opens. Check the transmission range of the unit: most wireless doorbells work at up to 50 m in the open air, but masonry walls and steel-frame construction cut the range significantly.
Fit the button to the wall or frame

Most wireless buttons come with a self-adhesive pad and two screws. For a permanent fix, use the screws: drill two pilot holes in the door frame or masonry. On masonry, use a 6 mm masonry plug. On a timber frame, drive the screws directly into the timber. Insert the batteries and screw the button to the fixing. The push button is low-voltage radio equipment; no mains power, no electrical isolation needed.

Plug the chime unit into a mains socket in the hallway or nearest convenient room. Most units pair automatically when the push button is pressed for the first time; some have a pairing button that must be held while the push button is pressed. Refer to the unit instructions for the pairing sequence. Test the range by walking to the door and pressing the button; the chime should sound reliably. If it does not, move the chime unit to a socket closer to the front door.

attrs.symptom: Chime does not sound when button is pressed
attrs.cause: Pairing was lost, or the range is too great through the building structure.
attrs.fix: Re-pair the units with the chime unit and the push button in the same room. Then move the chime to the target socket and test; if range is lost, try a repeater unit or a unit with a longer-range radio (433 MHz or 868 MHz models).

attrs.symptom: The chime sounds at random with no one pressing the button
attrs.cause: Interference from a neighbour's compatible wireless doorbell, or the push button has water ingress causing false triggers.
attrs.fix: Change the radio channel on both units. Check the push button for water ingress in a covered position; replace if damaged.
